items.title: Corse al buio dopo il cambio d'ora: gli OpenFit Air 2 di Shokz lasciano le orecchie libere
items.summary: Auricolari open-ear leggerissimi, da 7,2 grammi, che fanno sentire il mondo intorno a sé mentre si ascolta musica. Utili anche per un’attività all’aperto più sicura ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Alle sei di sera il parco è già buio. Con il ritorno dell'ora solare il tardo pomeriggio ha perso un'ora di luce e chi corre dopo il lavoro si ritrova su strade e ciclabili illuminate soltanto dai lampioni, quando ci sono . Una bici che arriva alle spalle si sente prima di vederla, a patto di avere le orecchie libere.

Su questa idea Shokz ha costruito i nuovi OpenFit Air 2 , auricolari true wireless open-ear, in modo da permettere di ascoltare il mondo attorno a sé non rinunciando alla qualità audio: un firma distintiva del brand.

I nuovi OpenFit Air 2 non entrano nel condotto uditivo, ma si agganciano all'orecchio con un archetto e appoggiano l'altoparlante davanti all'ingresso del canale, che resta aperto . In questo modo pur ascoltando la musica, il rumore di un motore o il passo di un altro runner possono essere avvertiti .

Lasciare l'orecchio aperto ha sempre avuto un prezzo in bassi e riservatezza. Shokz però ha risolto il problema con il sistema Bassphere, due altoparlanti circolari da 11,8 mm che rendono come un singolo driver da 16 mm , affiancati dall'algoritmo OpenBass 2.0.

L'altoparlante è inclinato di 30 gradi e la tecnologia DirectPitch indirizza il suono verso l'orecchio, limitando quello che sente chi sta accanto. Dall'app Shokz si sceglie tra quattro equalizzazioni preimpostate, compresa una modalità Private specifica per gli ambienti silenziosi.

Chi corre con auricolari wireless conosce il timore di vederne volare via uno a metà ripetuta, però l'archetto degli OpenFit Air 2 è un filo in lega di nichel-titanio da 0,75 mm, un materiale che si flette e torna in forma, e ogni auricolare pesa 7,2 grammi contro gli 8,7 del modello precedente. Tutto ciò che serve per mantenere ben saldo all’orecchio l’auricolare, ma se senza fastidi.

Al posto delle superfici touch ci sono pulsanti fisici sensibili alla pressione , così con le mani sudate o i guanti invernali un tocco involontario non mette in pausa la playlist. La certificazione IP55 protegge da sudore e pioggia .

Finito l'allenamento, gli stessi auricolari servono in ufficio o sui mezzi, senza contare che camminare in città potendo accorgersi dei rumori è molto utile per la sicurezza. Nelle chiamate lavorano due microfoni per auricolare, affiancati da un algoritmo di riduzione del rumore basato sull'intelligenza artificiale che comunque filtra il brusio di fondo , mentre il multipoint tiene collegati due dispositivi insieme , per esempio smartphone e PC. Con il Bluetooth 6.1 arrivano anche Fast Pair e Swift Pair, per abbinarli al volo a telefoni Android e computer Windows.

Con una ricarica dei nuovi Shokz OpenFit Air 2 si hanno fino a 8 ore di musica e 36 ore complessive con la custodia , che è anche più compatta del rispetto alla generazione precedente. Inoltre, 10 minuti di ricarica bastano per circa 3 ore di ascolto, abbastanza per l'uscita serale anche quando ci si accorge all'ultimo che la batteria è scarica.

Gli Shokz OpenFit Air 2 sono disponibili nei colori nero, bianco e Ice Blue. Si comprano sullo store italiano di Shokz e dai rivenditori autorizzati di elettronica e articoli sportivi, con due anni di garanzia e reso entro 30 giorni sul sito ufficiale.

items.title: Herdr has released native app
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50298436 Points: 6 # Comments: 0
items.content:
Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin . Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app . For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications.

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as:

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format.

Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves.

Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod.

This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.

The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments.

For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing .

Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI . Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.

Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.

Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages.

To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:

The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.

python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py .

items.title: Cormac McCarthy's Library
items.summary: Article URL: https://cormacmccarthy.lib.utk.edu/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50298318 Points: 8 # Comments: 1
items.content:
Anubis could not load its JavaScript. The server may be overloaded. Please reload the page to try again.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.

Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

items.content:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

items.title: Elicottero italiano cade in Bosnia, quattro militari morti
items.summary: Il velivolo era impegnato nella missione Althea. Le vittime facevano parte di Esercito e Croce rossa, tra loro anche una donna. I feriti sono 11. Cordoglio di Mattarella e Meloni
items.content:
L'imponente Chinook dell'Esercito italiano dal caratteristico doppio rotore improvvisamente prende ad avvitarsi su sé stesso in un movimento a spirale discendente mentre vola a bassa quota e si schianta rapidamente a terra in una campagna del distretto di Brčko, in Bosnia. A bordo ci sono 15 militari della missione Eufor Althea. Il bilancio è di quattro italiani morti: due dell'Esercito, il sergente Simone Ruggia e il sergente Claudio Marchesi, e due della Croce Rossa, il tenente Franco Adriano Zecchillo e il sergente Laura Procacci. Undici i feriti, nessuno rischia la vita. La Difesa ha immediatamente disposto l'invio di un'équipe medica per garantire loro il massimo supporto e aperto un'inchiesta per accertare le cause. Nell'area dell'incidente sono subito scattati i soccorsi, con l'intervento di vigili del fuoco e protezione civile oltre ai militari di Eufor. Sul terreno è rimasto l'elicottero a pezzi ed è risultato particolarmente complesso il lavoro di estrazione dei corpi dalle lamiere. Secondo le prime informazioni, le due vittime militari facevano parte del Comando Aviazione dell'Esercito di Viterbo: si tratterebbe del pilota e dello specialista dell'aeromobile, entrambi appartenenti al primo reggimento Antares di stanza nel capoluogo laziale. E sembra che il Chinook caduto fosse parti to per la Bosnia mercoledì mattina da Viterbo.

Cordoglio bipartisan della politica, con il presidente della Repubblica, Sergio Mattarella, che ha inviato un messaggio al capo di Stato Maggiore della Difesa, Luciano Portolano, esprimendo "profonda commozione: in questa triste circostanza, voglia rendersi interprete presso l'Esercito Italiano e il Corpo Militare della Croce Rossa dei miei sentimenti di cordoglio e di commossa solidarietà al dolore provocato da questo tragico evento, chiedendo loro di esprimere ai familiari delle vittime la mia vicinanza e solidarietà". L'incidente è avvenuto nel pomeriggio, in una zona dove non c'era maltempo. Le immagini riprese da terra e che circolano in rete mostrano un cielo appena velato. Il ministero della Difesa fa sapere che le cause dell'incidente "sono corso di accertamento". Tra le ipotesi c'è anche quella di un possibile urto con cavi ad alta tensione. Eufor spiega che il velivolo stava conducendo un "addestramento di routine". La forza condurrà "un'indagine approfondita e completa per accertare i fatti". L'ambasciatrice d'Italia in Bosnia-Erzegovina, Sarah Castellani, è andata sul posto: "non è ancora chiara - riferisce - la dinamica dell'incidente, che sarebbe avvenuto in fase di decollo dall'aeroporto di Brčko, quindi immediatamente dopo". Alcuni testimoni oculari raccontano che l'elicottero volava a bassa quota prima dello schianto e ha effettuato diverse virate prima di toccare terra. A prestare le prime cure sono i sanitari del distretto di Brčko, vicino al confine orientale con la Croazia, a circa 120 km dalla capitale Sarajevo. Il velivolo, racconta all'ANSA il sindaco Sinisa Milic, "è caduto in una zona disabitata, per fortuna, non lontano dalle prime case del villaggio di Gorica". Il Chinook è un elicottero costruito dalla Boeing nei primi anni '60 ed è stato impiegato massicciamente nella guerra in Vietnam dalla forze armate americane ma è tutt'ora impiegato da tanti Paesi per le sue elevate capacità di carico: può portare fino a 50 persone. Era uno dei mezzi della missione Eufor Althea a guida italiana dal gennaio di quest'anno col generale Maurizio Fronda. Un'operazione nata nel 2004 e che punta a stabilizzare una delle sei repubbliche nate dalla disgregazione della Jugoslavia, supportando le autorità locali ed addestrando le forze armate. Di Althea fanno parte 1.600 militari di 24 Paesi: quello italiano è il contingente più numeroso, sono circa 300. Il quartier generale è a Camp Budmir, vicino Sarajevo. Dalla politica sono arrivati sentimenti di cordoglio. "Il mio pensiero - ha dichiarato la premier Giorgia Meloni - va alle vittime, alle loro famiglie e a tutti coloro che, impegnati nella missione per la pace e la stabilità della regione, stanno vivendo ore di angoscia. A loro va la mia più sincera vicinanza e quella del governo italiano". Per il ministro della Difesa, Guido Crosetto, è un "dolore immenso: non esistono parole capaci di colmare una perdita così grande. Ai nostri militari che hanno perso la vita servendo il Paese va la riconoscenza dell'Italia intera". Il ministro degli Esteri Anonio Tajani è "profondamente addolorato". Ed anche la segretaria del Pd, Elly Schlein, ha espresso "vicinanza ai militari feriti e a tutte le Forze Armate italiane per questa tragedia".

items.title: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014)
items.summary: Article URL: https://journal.animationstudies.org/article/id/66/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50297089 Points: 44 # Comments: 7
items.content:
Keywords: animation, militarism, Miyazaki, nationalism, non-killing policy, war

How to Cite: Akimoto, D., (2014) “A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso ( Kurenai no Buta )”, Animation Studies Journal 9(1). doi: https://doi.org/10.64864/a85b8d7f-b345-4fd3-a0ff-4f1b600c9b97

Introduction Historically, animated cartoons and movies have been used as ‘propaganda’ in war (Roffat 2011). Some animated films, however, contribute to conveying an anti-war pacifist point of view (Takai 2011). As such, the film Porco Rosso (1992) can be categorized as “anti-war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 144). Although Miyazaki has been attracted by seaplanes designed and manufactured during the period between the First World War and the Second World War (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72), this film conveys the important memory of war, especially the interwar era and the post-Cold War world. Indeed, in an interview just before the release of Porco Rosso , Miyazaki stated that the film is relevant to the Gulf War, and referred to the Yugoslav Wars as ethnic and nationalistic conflicts (Miyazaki 1996, p. 519; Miyazaki 2002, p. 95). In this context, the film forwards Miyazaki’s anti-war message. This paper examines Porco Rosso ( Kurenai no Buta ), which is based on 15 pages of Hikotei Jidai ( The Golden Age of the Flying Boat) , a comic created by Hayao Miyazaki and released in the animation journal, Model Graphics , No.14-16 in 1990 (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72). A synopsis of the comic story is literally “typed” at the beginning of Porco Rosso , as follows: “This motion picture is set over the Mediterranean Sea in an age when seaplanes ruled the waves. It tells a story of a valiant pig, who fought against flying pirates, for his pride, for his lover, and for his fortune. The name of the hero of our story is Crimson Pig.” Scholarship on this film has focused on issues of “war and peace,” especially in terms of the “non-war” ( hisen ) message (e.g. Okuda 2003). Similarly, Kazami et al (2002), among others, (Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provide some answers to the central question of the film: Why did Porco turn into a pig? The primary reason is that he was traumatized by the war. Building on Kazami et al’s work, this paper attributes the reason that Porco became a pig to the following three aspects: “man, the state and war” (Waltz, 1959). According Kenneth Waltz, theorist of international politics, the causes of war occur on three levels: individual, domestic, and international. Like Waltz, I argue here that Porco became a pig because he hates the following three factors: man (egoism), the state (nationalism) and war (militarism). Accordingly, my analysis of Porco Rosso is situated in the framework of peace research and international relations, such as non-killing philosophy, soft power/hard power, and conflict prevention/conflict resolution. Methodology In the field of animation studies, animation films by Studio Ghibli have been frequently analyzed as a case study. Ghibli animation films are “often considered as artistic productions, both entertaining and meaningful” (Gan 2009, p. 36). There are a large number of publications on the Studio Ghibli’s films, particularly those directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004), for instance, examined Miyazaki’s works in comparison with the animated cartoons of Osamu Tezuka, the creator of Astro Boy (1963). Miyazaki’s films also have been discussed compared with Disney animation. For instance, Kaori Yoshida (2011) offered a comparative analysis on Disney’s Pocahontas (1995) and Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke (1997) in terms of national identity. Moreover, some scholars (e.g. Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provided comprehensive thematic or structural analyses of Miyazaki’s films. However, earlier studies on Miyazaki animation, or Miyazaki-related animation films, do not necessarily focus on the issue of war and peace. Therefore, this paper offers an analysis of Miyazaki-related animation films in terms of war and peace (Table 1). Although the Miyazaki-related films in Table 1 do not directly deal with war themselves, all of them are related to war and peace to a certain extent. Hols: Prince of the Sun (1968) was released in the middle of the Vietnam War (1965-1975) and some combat scenes of the film represent the war. Miyazaki was involved as an animator in the creation of the film with director Isao Takahata, a friend and colleague. Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984) is a masterpiece, and the film reflects the international politics during the Cold War. The Giant Warrior ( kyoshinhei ) that caused an apocalyptic war, or the Seven Days of Fire, functions as a symbol of nuclear weaponry. The confrontation between Pejite and Tolmekia, the two powerful countries in the story can similarly be regarded as reflection of the Cold War bipolar structure (Akimoto 2014a). Laputa: Castle in the Sky (1986) was also created during the middle of the Cold War. The number of nuclear warheads in the world reached its peak in the mid-1980s, and the military technology of the legendary castle, Laputa, also symbolizes nuclear weapons. In this film, the word, “peace” is used only one time by Muska, who tries to conquer the world by taking possession of Laputa’s military technology. Obviously, this is a “political satire” by Miyazaki (Akimoto 2014b). Grave of the Fireflies (1988), a fictional film about a Japanese boy and his little sister at the end of the Pacific War (1941-1945), was not directed by Miyazaki but instead by Isao Takahata, another Studio Ghibli director (Akimoto 2014c), but reflects similar anti-war sentiment. In the post-Cold War context, Miyazaki produced Porco Rosso (1992) which depicts the interwar period (1919-1939) of the Adriatic Sea in conjunction with the Yugoslavian War (1991). Miyazaki contributed to the creation of Whisper of the Heart (1994) that has a passing reference to the Second World War (1939-1945). Princess Mononoke (1997) deals with Japanese civil war as well as confrontation between humans and animals. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004) and the latest film, The Wind Rises (2013) are related to the 2003 Iraq War, and the Asia Pacific War (1931-1945) (Akimoto 2014d; Akimoto 2014e). Thus, the films in which Miyazaki or Studio Ghibli is involved can be analyzed from a perspective of peace research (peace studies), an academic field which examines causes of war and conditions for peace. While ethical and legal issues need to be carefully taken into consideration when teaching Japanese animation (McLelland 2013), Studio Ghibli animation films can be useful as educational materials at the university level (Yonemura 2003, p. 10), particularly in the fields of both peace research and peace education. From the perspective of peace research, Porco Rosso makes a particularly rich case study, particularly because Miyazaki won the best feature film award in the 1993 Annecy International Animation Film Festival (Annecy.org 2013). Due to the award, which is one of the most internationally prestigious animation film festivals, the film was internationally acclaimed, and Miyazaki characterized as “Walt Disney Nippon” (Christin 1997, p. 184). Most reviews of and scholarship on Porco Rosso tend toward general analysis, lacking a specific focus on war and peace (e.g. Animage 1992, 2011; Kazami et al. 2002; Okuda 2003; Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008). Moreover, Miyazaki himself has made similar comments on his own work (Miyazaki 1996, 1997, 2013). Yet, none of the earlier studies of the film have investigated them from a perspective of peace research. In order to examine Porco Rosso , which conveys a similar anti-war message to The Wind Rises ( Kaze Tachinu ) (2013), which narrates Japan’s interwar period and war responsibility (Akimoto 2013a), this paper employs an interdisciplinary approach which combines peace research with animation studies. As an analytical method, this paper combines keyword analysis described above with sequence analysis of character’s lines as well as historical events. The sequence analysis is useful tool to examine timeline sequence (Abbott 1995) and it is applicable to film studies with a particular focus on character’s lines in historical context. Accordingly, the five main characters as well as historical background of this film need to be overviewed in this section. First, the hero of this film is a pig, Porco Rosso who flies in his crimson seaplane, SAVOIA S-21. As a bounty hunter, he cracks down on Aero Viking (Sky Pirates) in the Adriatic Sea after the First World War. He used to be a human (Marco Paggot) and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force, but he decided to leave the army after the war and cursed himself, turning into a pig. As I outline below, Porco was traumatized by his experiences in the war (Animage 2011, p. 35-37). Second, Madam Gina, a childhood friend of Porco and a madam of Hotel Adriano, is one of the two heroines of this film. In the film, it is said that pilots in the Mediterranean Sea tend to fall in love with her and visit Hotel Adriano for her song. She was married to three pilots who were all members of the Flying Club she organized as a child, but all of them died in the Great War, or in a flight accident. Gina is in secret love with Porco and vice versa (ibid, p. 54-57). Third, Fiyo Piccolo, the other heroine, is a 17-year old female mechanic and the granddaughter of Master Piccolo. She repairs Porco’s seaplane and develops an adolescent infatuation with him (ibid, 43-45). Fourth, Donald Curtis, an American pilot and Porco’s rival, is hired by Aero Viking to fight against Porco. He is a competent pilot and has an ambition to first become a Hollywood movie star, and then US President afterwards. Curtis falls in love with Gina at first sight and falls for Fiyo next (ibid, pp. 48-51). Fifth, the Mamma Aiutos, one of the largest Aero Vikings in the Adriatic Sea, steals and kidnaps for a living after the First World War (ibid, p. 63-65). This study examines the five character’s lines in the following historical context as demonstrated by Table 2 below. At a macro level, the chronology of the interwar period as the historical background for the film needs to be taken into consideration, as this background is crucial in understanding the content of this film. At a micro level, key scenes and main characters’ lines of the film will be examined. This is also imperative to comprehend the implications of the film for the issue of war and peace. The sequence of the nine most significant scenes in the film are as follows: 1) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos 2) Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” 3) Gina’s Life in War and Peace 4) Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War 5) Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane 6) The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” 7) Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” 8) The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? 9) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle The main characters’ dialogue in these nine sections accordingly constitute the primary source to be carefully investigated, in combination with my earlier argument, and relevant publications as secondary source in the context of the interwar period. The sequence analysis of the film and characters’ lines will be examined by using keywords in peace research and international politics. Findings 1. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos The film begins with a scene in which the main character, Porco Rosso (who seems to be enjoying his vacation – drinking wine and taking a nap at a beach), wakes up with a phone call for an emergency. He works as a contract combat fighter pilot in order to crack down on flying pirates and gangs, such as the Mamma Aiutos. Although he left the Italian Army, he works for peace and security of the Adriatic Sea in place of Mussolini’s National Fascist Party. Italy was one of the member states of Security Council on the League of Nations (1920-1946), but its collective security system did not function, and eventually could not prevent the occurrence of the Manchurian Incident (1931) and the Abyssinian Crisis, or the Second Italy-Ethiopian War (1935-1936). In this way, Porco’s work in the film can be seen as police operations, to maintain peace and safety during the time period. As I will discuss, the international system is more anarchic in this age, and the police and military forces of Italy were not necessarily efficient or functional, leading to the populace in the film making a contract with Porco to crack down on flying pirates. In the field of peace research, Glenn D. Paige (2009) examines “non-killing” as an analytical terminology. This paper, therefore, uses the term “non-killing” as a research keyword. In the first battle scene of this film, Porco demonstrates his “non-killing” policy. In order to make money, save hostages, and to keep peace on the Adriatic Sea, Porco decides to crack down on the Mamma Aiutos, but remains true to his “non-killing” principles. In the battle scene with the Mamma Aiutos, it comes to light that Porco has no intention to kill the gang. Instead, he tries to shoot their aircraft without causing serious damage to the pirates and hostages, and then demands that they should leave half the money and hostages in exchange for their lives. Although he calls a bluff saying: “Or I’ll kill all of you,” his policy is very clear early on in the film. 2. Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” Female characters in this film (Gina and Fiyo) were depicted as attractive and peaceful heroines. In terms of gender studies, Kuwabara (2007) sheds light on the concept of “feminism” and the meaning of the crimson color reflected in the movie. In an application of politics and international relations, Tomoko Shimizu (2004) analyzes Ghibli animation in terms of “soft power” in the post-Cold War era. The concept of “soft power” was proposed by Joseph Nye, a Harvard Professor and political scientist. As opposed to “hard power” which based on military power, “soft power” can be defined as “the ability to get what you want through attraction rather than coercion or payments. It arises from the attractiveness of a country’s culture, political ideas, and policies” (Nye 2004, p. x). In this framework, Japanese animation can be understood as Japanese “soft power,” which works to enhance Japan’s international image and attractiveness as national interest. For example, Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004) used the term “power of Japan animation” to contextualize the Japanese animation industry, which has lasted more than 85 years. Likewise, William Armour (2011) described Japanese animation and manga for learning Japanese language as “soft power pedagogy” (p. 125). In this fashion, Gina and Fiyo, as the two main female characters, become exemplary of the concept of “soft power.” After the battle, Porco drops in the Hotel Adriano run by Madam Gina, a childhood friend. In the film, it is stressed that Gina’s charismatic beauty and elegance prevents violent conflict by air pirates from occurring around her hotel. For instance, Donald Curtis, an American air fighter as a rival of Porco, says: “She is quite a woman… Air pirates and bounty hunters alike leave their quarrels outside.” The reason why the flying gang never fights near the Hotel Adriano can be inferred by the fact that the gang know that Gina lost her husband in WWI, which I will discuss in the next section. When tension builds between Porco and a drunken gang, Gina swiftly intervenes and prevents confrontation from escalating. Gina says to the gang: “Quite a distinguished gathering! You boys must be planning something… Always glad to see you, but no war games here, OK?” One of the gang responses: “We know, Gina. We don’t work within 50 kilometers of here”. Another gang continues: “We’re even polite to the pig!” And then Gina says: “That’s my boys.” This scene reflects Gina’s charm as “soft power” in contrast to gang’s “hard power” results in peaceful conflict resolution. As such, conflict resolution can be divided into the following four phases: 1) preventive diplomacy (conflict prevention), 2) peacemaking (peace enforcement), 3) peacekeeping, and 4) peacebuilding, as proposed by Boutros Ghali, the former UN Secretary General, in his “An Agenda For Peace” (United Nations 1992). In application of the process of conflict resolution, Gina’s approach in the Hotel Adriano can be categorized as “preventive diplomacy” (conflict prevention) by her soft power. 3. Gina’s Life in War and Peace In opposition to her otherwise peaceful and graceful characteristics, Gina’s life seems to be swayed by the time period, especially the war. Gina literally hates war (Isaka 2001, p. 156). The film implies that Gina lost her first husband because of the First World War. The war was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand of Australia, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. About one month later, Austria-Hungary as an ally of Germany declared a war on Serbia, a key ally of Russia. The two blocks involved the entire Europe and led to the Great War. Originally, Italy was a part of the Central Powers (Triple Alliance) with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but it eventually joined the Allies (Triple Entente) led by the United Kingdom, France, and Russia. This was how the Italian Air Force had to fight against the Austria-Hungary Force in the Adriatic Sea (Matsuki 2013, p. 46). At the beginning of the First World War, the number of combat planes of the Italian Navy was 15, and that of Austria-Hungary was 22. When Italy declared war against Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915, Italy possessed only 15 combat airplanes, whereas Austria-Hungary already had about 90 warplanes ready to attack Venice. At the end of the war, the total number of the Italian Navy was as many as 1,630, whereas that of Austria-Hungary was around 650. During the war, Italy lost 121 fighter planes and destroyed 132 Austrian-Hungarian combat planes. The most important base for the Italian Navy was Venice, which was assaulted 42 times and 1,037 bombs were dropped on the city. The number of the combat planes involved in the war in the Adriatic Sea can be shown as Table 3. The death toll of Italian pilots from the battle in the Adriatic Sea can be inferred by the number of the loss, and Gina’s husband could be included. Gina has married two other pilots who were also killed in combat. She tells Porco: “One died in the war, one in the Atlantic, and the third in Asia.” Porco asks: “They found him?” And Gina replies: “I got a call today. They found his remains in Bengal. It’s been three years. I’ve got no more tears left.” To which Porco replies: “The good ones always get killed.” Their conversation indicates that Gina’s husbands died due to flight accidents or fell in the line of duty for the Italian Air Force, which Porco left. This is the reason why Gina hates “war” and, moreover, tries to stop Porco from going to the air fight. Gina’s second husband was likely a similarly capable pilot who possibly met with an accident during the flight for adventure or international seaplane race, such as the so-called “Schneider Trophy. ” The award was named after Jacques Schneider, a French industrial manager, and the races were held from 1913 to 1931 (Table 4). As Table 4 demonstrates, Italian pilots won the Schneider Trophy three times, and six races took place in Italy itself. Given Porco’s flying skill as the “ace” of the Italian Air Force, it is entirely likely that Porco or the other members of the Flying Club organized by Gina might have participated in the Schneider Trophy. According to Pierre Pecastaingts (1996), there were no casualties in the race of the Schneider Trophy, training for the races led to fatal accidents, killing five Italian pilots. Accordingly, it is possible that Gina’s second husband met flight accident in preparation for a contest not unlike the Schneider Trophy. Or they might have died in the flying training or military mission of the Italian Air Force. In either scenario, Gina’s wartime and peacetime experiences have been influenced by airplanes, and contributes to her fears for Porco. 4. Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War Although Porco “fights” for bounty money as a seaplane pilot, he demonstrates antipathy towards the state (nationalism/fascism) and militarism (war). After he left the Hotel Adriano, he goes to a bank. A military parade full of national flags on tanks with a militaristic music took place on the street beside the bank. When Porco enters the bank to withdraw some money, a bank clerk mentions that it “must be nice to make that much money… How about making a contribution to the people with a Patriot Bond?” To which Porco replies, “I’m not a person.” The “patriot bond” is meant to be a war bond, necessary to prepare and wage wars by the Italian government. Here, Porco clearly opposes financial contribution to fascism and militarism. Also, this scene reminds Japanese audience of Japan’s response to the 1990 Gulf Crisis, during which, the Japanese government was reluctant to making financial contributions to the US-led multinational forces (Akimoto 2013b). After he leaves the bank, Porco walks down to buy weapons for his seaplane. In accordance with his non-killing policy, Porco purchases only light weapons, so a young weapon trader asks Porco to buy more strong weapons saying: “Just regular bullets? Not high-explosives, or armor-piercing?” Yet, Porco turns him down, replying: “Listen, kid. We’re not fighting a war out there. See you.” Immediately thereafter, the young trader asks his boss: “Hey. Boss… How is war different from bounty hunting?” And the boss sarcastically replies that: “War profiteers are villains. Bounty hunters are just stupid.” These scenes regarding “war bond” and “military weapons” foreground Porco’s hatred towards nationalism (fascism) and militarism, and works to highlight Miyazaki’s own anti-war pacifism and his viewpoint on the 1990 Gulf Crisis and the 1991 Gulf War. 5. Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane When Porco flies to go to have his seaplane fixed at the Piccolo’s, Curtis, an American seaplane pilot hired by the Mamma Aiutos suddenly attacks Porco. Yet, Porco tries to avoid one-on-one fight mainly because of the engine trouble, but fundamentally due to his non-killing policy. This is how Curtis succeeds in damaging Porco’s seaplane and it leads to a major repair at the Piccolo’s. Fiyo, Piccolo’s granddaughter, designs and plans the repair and rebuilding of Porco’s seaplane. That only female workers who are related to Piccolo are involved in the creation of the new plane is suggestive of the effects of the Great Depression, wherein men travelled for work outside the town or to join the military. 6. The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” Porco’s anti-fascist attitude is reflected by the fact that Porco Rosso also makes reference to Casablanca (1942), an American romantic drama, which portrays the fight against the Nazis during the Second World War as “war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 137-144). Similarities between the two films include characters, but the purpose of Casablanca is considered to justify US participation in the war in Europe (ibid, p. 140), whereas that of Porco Rosso is oppose killing and war in general. In this regard, its fundamental political message of the film is not only anti-fascism, but also anti-war pacifism. When Porco watches a movie at a theatre, Ferrarin, Porco’s old friend in the Italian Air Force, warns that there are warrants out on Porco for “treason, illegal entry… decadence, pornography and being a lazy pig.” Ferrarin suggests that Porco should come back to the Air Force before the authorities seize his plane. However, Porco flatly declines this offer, saying: “Better a pig than a Fascist.” In response, Ferrarin warns again to “Be careful. They won’t bother with a court of law.” This scene is telling, in that Porco, who used to be a war hero, decided to become and remain a pig because he did not want to be a fascist who supported nationalistic militarism during that time. After their conversation in the theater, as Ferrarin mentioned, Porco and Fiyo are being tailed by the Fascist Secret Police. Fiyo insists that she needs to accompany Porco as a mechanic, but Porco opposed her plan at first. Yet, Fiyo persuaded Porco to come along with him, and Porco finally says: “Take out the right machine gun. I don’t care how small your bottom is. It won’t fit between them.” This implies that in addition to his anti-fascist stance, Porco is also a feminist who respects women, at the sacrifice of weapons on his airplane. When Porco and Fiyo are about to take off, the Fascist Secret Police shoot the plane, and Porco discharges a machine gun at them as warning shots, but does not intend to kill them. These scenes are an additional reflection of Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy, is situated in Miyazaki’s anti-war pacifism. 7. Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” The Mamma Aiutos and other air pirates ambush and take Porco and Fiyo as hostages at Porco’s hideout. When the pirates say they are going to destroy Porco’s fighter plane, Fiyo, as a designer of the plane, strongly objects. She makes an eloquent speech to the boss of the Mamma Aiutos about how brave and proud seaplane pilots are, and how noble and respectful the gang should be. Her attractiveness as Piccolo’s chief plane designer, as well as her peaceful means of conflict resolution, save the plane in addition to Porco’s life. In place of the Mamma Aiutos, Curtis says that he will have a one-on-one battle with Porco. Again, Miyazaki places an emphasis on the soft power of female characters, in brokering peaceful conflict resolution. Where Gina showed her soft power for “conflict prevention” as preventive diplomacy, Fiyo’s courageous approach led to the peaceful and successful ‘conflict resolution’ which prevents confrontation from escalating into violence. This is how Miyazaki makes audience remember the importance of peaceful conflict resolution based on a “non-killing” philosophy. 8. The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? The night before the rematch with Curtis, Fiyo asks Porco why he turned into a pic, but he does not directly answer her question. According to Fiyo, her father was in the same unit as a Flight Lieutenant Marco Paggot, or, Porco when he was still human and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force. Fiyo’s favorite story about the war is that Porco jumped off a cliff to rescue an enemy pilot in a war, which is indicative that Porco was an anti-war humanist long before he became a pig. In the evening, Porco finally tells what happened and implies how he turned into a pig in the last summer of the war. This episode is one of the most important scenes in the film, according to most scholars (Kazami et al. 2002, p. 140; Kano 2006, p. 163; Kiridoshi 2008, p. 79). Porco flew with his old friend Berlini, who had just married two days before the final patrol over the Adriatic. During the flight, they were attacked by Austrian fighter planes. Porco did not have enough leeway to assist Berlini, and turned out to be the only survivor of the battle. Porco was so exhausted and traumatized that he hallucinated and saw other dead pilots going up to the cemetery of fighter planes. Berlini was one of Gina’s husbands, and Porco was the best man at their wedding. The film implies that Porco could not forgive himself for forsaking Berlini and this is one of the main reasons why he decided to cast a spell to turn himself into a pig. It is also understandable that he came to hate humans, the government, and the war that killed his most of his friends and cursed his life. Through his experience, he actually saw that war makes people ugly, egoistic and inhumane. In short, the war, on the basis of egoism, nationalism and militarism, traumatized Porco so much that he decided to turn himself into a pig. Japanese people tend to regard pigs as uglier than any other animal, but ironically, Miyazaki in the film strongly suggests that humans sometimes can be uglier than pigs. 9. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle Even in the final battle wagering Fiyo, Porco sticks to his “non-killing” principle and does not attempt to kill Curtis. Indeed, the boss of the Mamma Aiutos offers commentaries that: “The Pig’s not a killer,” and that “The damn fool thinks this isn’t war!” Porco’s strategy is to let Curtis shoot first until he runs out of bullets. Owing to the “barrel roll” flying manoeuver which made Porco “the Ace of the Adriatic,” Porco gets a chance to shoot Curtis’s plane, but he still does not discharge the machine gun. Porco only waits for an opportunity to place a few non-fatal shots into the engine so that he does not need to take Curtis’s life. After Porco and Curtis run out of bullets, they end up in physical altercation. This scene could be considered as animated violence, as Princess Mononoke (Mononoke Hime) (1997) is often criticized as full of “violence and bleeding” (Kusanagi 2003, p. 266-267), but at the same time, it illustrates the foolishness of fighting. At the end, the fight itself turns out to be more of a sport (boxing match) than actual violence or bloodshed. Eventually, Porco wins the boxing match and Gina comes to announce “ceasefire” noting: “Ok, the party is over. The Italian Air Force is coming. Get out of here, everyone.” Again, it is emphasized that Gina, on the basis of her soft power, takes leadership for the ceasefire and prevents the gangs from triggering unnecessary collateral conflicts after the battle. As was the case at the Hotel Adriano, Gina’s role here is conflict prevention based on preventive diplomacy. Thus, Miyazaki stresses the significance of peaceful conflict resolution as “non-killing” through to the end of the film. Conclusion It has been emphasized and confirmed that Porco became a pig not only because of war (militarism) and the state (nationalism/fascism), or but also because of negative human nature (egoism). This is how he came to detest being a human. In addition, Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy has not changed until the very ending of this film. This film also stresses “soft power” of Gina and Fiyo in the conflict prevention, conflict resolution and ceasefire. In the epilogue of the film, even after the failure of the crackdown by the Italian Air Force, Porco never turns up in front of Fiyo. Instead, Fiyo becomes good friends with Gina as they underwent the subsequent war and turmoil. Curtis became a movie star in the United States and other flying pirates still visit the Hotel Adriano. It is not a gloomy epilogue, but what happened to Porco still remains a mystery. Historically, it is logical to infer that Fiyo and Gina survived the Second World War. Porco’s antipathy towards fascism and war has been consistent throughout this movie, so it is unlikely that Porco would return to the Italian Air Force during the this conflict. However, according to Miyazaki, Porco is supposed to be the fourth husband of Gina (Kano 2006, p. 163) and it is suggested that Porco could be involved in the war not for his country, but for Gina, Fiyo and his friends, and this might be the reason why Porco never shows up in the epilogue narrated by Fiyo. In conclusion, through the comical and romantic animated storyline, this movie conveys Miyazaki’s antiwar pacifism, non-killing philosophy, and the memory of war. items.title: Serie A: Fiorentina-Atalanta, spettacolo e gol ma solo un punto a testa
items.summary: Finisce 2-2. Classifica ferma ma il bel gioco lascia ben sperare per il futuro
items.content:
Davanti ai propri tifosi la Fiorentina non torna alla vittoria, ma contro l'Atalanta ferma la serie di sconfitte e conquista un punto che può fare comunque morale. Una gara, terminata 2-2, dai due volti: primo tempo dell'Atalanta e ripresa dei viola. I padroni di casa addirittura riescono a passare in vantaggio, ma non capaci di reggere fino alla fine. Dall'altra parte Sarri è in piena emergenza ma a tratti si vede un'Atalanta capace d'imporre il proprio gioco, anche se forse è poco cinica davanti alla porta di De Gea.

Nel primo tempo la Fiorentina parte subito col piede sull'acceleratore cercando il gol del vantaggio con velocità, pressing sul portatore di palla e con le giocate di Mastantuono e Njie; i tiri in porta di Joao Mario, Jimenez, Brescianini e Fagioli. Non trova, però, la fortuna sperata. Per imprecisione, per poca convinzione e troppa frenesia. Con giocatori che spesso non si smarcano e non danno soluzioni alternative al portatore di palla. Dall'altra parte l'Atalanta si fa sorprendere inizialmente dalla partenza dei viola, ma col passare dei minuti riesce prima a rispondere in contropiede e poi a conquistare il centrocampo: allo scadere del primo tempo passa in vantaggio. Al 41' l'azione sviluppata sulla sinistra con l'assist di Zalewski per De Ketelaere al centro dell'area dove l'attaccante batte facilmente De Gea. Un minuto dopo la Dea addirittura ha la possibilità di raddoppiare: palla al centro dell'area viola, dove nessun difensore gigliato salta ma c'è Krstovic che da due passi cerca l'angolo basso alla destra di De Gea che si oppone con un grande parata a terra. A inizio secondo tempo non rientra in campo l'arbitro La Penna per un infortunio e il suo posto viene preso dal quarto uomo Marinelli. Vanoli provava a cambiare la sua Fiorentina, lasciando negli spogliatoi uno spento Fagioli per Oulai. Al 48' ci prova Mastantuono con una gran punizione dalla distanza ma la palla esce di un soffio a lato. E al 53' arriva il pareggio della Fiorentina (che aveva iniziato il secondo tempo chiudendo l'Atalanta nella sua metà campo): cross dalla destra di Jimenz sul palo lontano dove sbuca Njie che salta indisturbato e di testa segna il gol del pareggio. La Fiorentina ci crede, continua a spingere e al 61'st trova il gol del vantaggio: Joao Mario prende palla sull'out di sinistra, si accentra e dal limite tira in porta dove prima trova la deviazione di Obric e poi quella del portiere Carnesecchi che tocca la palla con il piede ma non riesce a evitare il gol. L'Atalanta di Sarri però non si butta giù, resta in partita e al 74'st trova il gol del pareggio: Zalewski fa partire un tiro secco e preciso che si insacca all'angolino con De Gea rimasto fermo al centro della porta. Nel finale di partita De Gea compie due grandissime parate in volo per evitare la beffa finale. Un pareggio che non contenta nessuna delle due squadre in termini di classifica ma che, per entrambe, ha messo in evidenza progressi nel gioco in vista dei prossimi incontri.

items.title: The Great American Rascal: Tom Sawyer at 150
items.summary: Article URL: https://claremontreviewofbooks.com/the-great-american-rascal/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50296947 Points: 41 # Comments: 12
items.content:
The Adventures of Tom Sawyer marks its 150th anniversary this year. It was first published in 1876, the centennial year of the American Founding. The novel itself marked its own kind of founding moment for American literature, which had been laboring—to borrow a phrase from The Federalist —under the “arrogant pretensions of the European.” America may have broken free of Great Britain in 1776, but we remained enthralled to Europe culturally for much longer. In his 1837 essay “The American Scholar,” Ralph Waldo Emerson lamented that American writers had “listened too long to the courtly muses of Europe” and scraped by on the “sere remains of foreign harvests.”

Emerson then issued what Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr. dubbed an “Intellectual Declaration of Independence.” For Emerson, “genius looks forward.” He wanted to find, as he put it in his 1844 essay “The Poet,” the Homer of America—a bard “with a tyrannous eye” who “knew the value of our incomparable materials, and saw, in the barbarism and materialism of the times, another carnival of the same gods whose picture [one] so much admires in Homer.” In much the same spirit, Walt Whitman longed for a “democratic literature” filled with “archetypal poems” that could thicken America’s cultural “marrow.”

American men of letters such as James Fenimore Cooper, Edgar Allan Poe, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow each made their contributions in the struggle to pull away culturally from Europe. But it was Samuel Clemens—Mark Twain—who made the decisive revolutionary break. In the words of the critic William Dean Howells, “I knew them all…our sages, poets, seers, critics, humorists; they were like one another and like other literary men; but Clemens was sole, incomparable, the Lincoln of our literature.”

With The Adventures of Tom Sawyer , his first novel, Twain offered a new archetypal hero for democracy. He replaced the squeaky-clean “model boys” that tended to star in mid-19th century serials like McGuffey’s Eclectic Readers and Peter Parley’s Magazine , to which Twain’s father had subscribed. Tom is an altogether more vivid, more fully realized kind of boy. He leaps off the page from the very first word of the novel, which is his name, printed in huge capital letters: “‘TOM!’” yells his Aunt Polly. “‘What’s gone with that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!” An early review from England criticized the “queer Americanizing of the language.”

The frontier vernacular was part of the point, however, as distinctive as the behavior of the boy hero. In the first chapter, on day one alone, Tom hides in a closet gorging on forbidden jam, runs away from Aunt Polly’s whipping, plays hooky from school to go swimming, opportunistically steals sugar at the dinner table, lies to his aunt about being in school, and gets into a fight with a new boy in town because he is well-dressed and wearing shoes. Twain announces outright that Tom “was not the Model Boy of the village.” He reinforces this theme so well throughout the novel that the Brooklyn Public Library excluded The Adventures of Tom Sawyer from their reading room upon its publication.

Other reactions were more appreciative and far-seeing. Moncure Conway, Twain’s friend and literary agent in London, observed: “The book will no doubt be a favorite with boys, for whom it must in good part have been intended; but next to boys we should say that it might be most prized by philosophers and poets!” Conway was among the few (even to this day) to grasp the deeper import of the novel, which is often wrongfully dismissed as simply a humorously nostalgic tale for children. But one philosopher who seems to have appreciated Tom Sawyer ’s many subtleties was Friedrich Nietzsche. He wrote to his friend Franz Overbeck in 1879 that his mother had been reading it to him so he could rest his strained eyes. In another letter, this one to the novelist Paul Rée, he declared that he preferred Mark Twain’s American “silliness” to German “cleverness.”

Perhaps there is a Nietzschean streak to Tom. He certainly delights in upending the staid morality of St. Petersburg, Missouri, whose inhabitants Twain describes as “grave, unromantic men.” They are locked into the drab ritual formalities of what Leo Strauss called the joyless pursuit of joy: grinding labor without much delight in profit; dutiful rote piety without genuine religious passion. Tom shocks and offends the sensibilities of almost everyone around him, but he also enlivens their world and broadens their horizons, turning the dour solemnities of the town into a backdrop for his playfully mischievous imagination. The most famous scene in the book is the one in which Aunt Polly punishes Tom for playing hooky by making him whitewash her fence on a Saturday morning. In late edits, Twain enhanced the fence from four feet high to mythic proportions—a forbidding structure nine feet tall and 30 yards wide. Yet Tom somehow convinces the other boys in town that whitewashing may not be work after all.

“What do you call work?” Tom asks his peer Ben Rogers. “Why ain’t that work?” replies Ben. “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t,” says Tom. “All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.” Tom neither denies nor affirms that whitewashing is work, shrouding the act in an air of mystery and bending reality by the sheer force of his will until his friends look with envy at a dull chore. An engrossed Tom refuses Ben’s initial pleas to take a turn by telling him Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence, lying that he had to turn away his half-brother, Sid, and the enslaved Jim, who wanted to try. Soon the boys pour out all their worldly goods at Tom’s feet, essentially paying him for their own labor and putting three fine coats of paint on the entire fence.

Twain calls this a “slaughter of innocents,” in which Tom discovers “it’s not such a hollow world after all.” He learns, writes Twain, that “Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do.” He resolves Karl Marx’s problem of the manual worker’s alienation from his labor, yet he still makes a good capitalist profit. It’s a win-win. Harry V. Jaffa, in his definitive 1972 essay on the novel, “Tom Sawyer: Hero of Middle America” (collected in The Conditions of Freedom: Essays in Political Philosophy , 1975), captures the enormity of Tom’s ruse: “What he realizes is pure profit, purer profit indeed than Karl Marx ever imagined in his wildest polemics, against the iniquity of surplus value.”

The whitewashing episode is just the first of Tom’s many successful bids to jolt his quiet town into levity. He is at his impish best in church. As Alexis de Tocqueville recognized, Americans’ religious zeal can sometimes be “so methodical, so calculated that it would seem that the head rather than the heart leads them to the foot of the altar.” St. Petersburg’s congregants labor under the weight of sermons that “[deal] in limitless fire and brimstone and [thin] the predestined elect down to a company so small as to be hardly worth saving.”

Tom comes to the rescue, however, and finds a way to relieve the ceaseless fretting over predestination. He uses the loot he got from the whitewashing incident to buy Bible verse tickets, given to children in exchange for memorizing verses. Tom, who rattles off dialogue from The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood by heart, goes to church “snarling” and struggles to recite so much as a sentence from the Beatitudes. So, what a surprise—“the most stunning surprise of the decade”—when he presents enough tickets to claim the coveted prize of an illustrated Doré Bible, awarded to the pupil for memorizing 2,000 verses.

The revered local celebrity, Judge Thatcher, gives a predictably moralistic lecture forecasting that when Tom becomes a great man he’ll owe it all to the lessons of his Sunday School days. Then the judge asks Tom to name the first two apostles. Tom hesitates but finally offers: “David and Goliath.” Still, despite the obvious fraud, Judge Thatcher eventually conceives a “high opinion” of Tom for some of his more gallant exploits. By the end of the novel, he reiterates his prediction that Tom will be a great man on a par even with George Washington. (You can almost hear Nietzsche laughing out loud.)

But nothing revives the church as much as Tom’s triumphant return from the dead. He, Huck Finn, and Joe Harper have absconded to Jackson’s Island, where they play pirates and Indians, smoke pipes, swim, and soon grow homesick. Tom, aware from a secret scouting expedition that the town is in mourning, devises an elaborate plan for the gang to attend their own funeral the following Sunday. When the boys appear, a packed church rejoices and sings the Doxology “with a triumphant burst” that “[shakes] the rafters.” The congregants know they’ve been hoaxed, but they don’t care: Tom’s antics have inspired an ecstasy that the pastor’s droning sermons never could. “As the ‘sold’ congregation trooped out they said they would almost be willing to be made ridiculous again to hear Old Hundred sung like that once more.”

items.title: Happy Halloween, ma che festa da paura è diventata? SPECIALE
items.summary: Dai costumi per neonati al labirinto di mais, dal lucidalabbra magnetico alla cravatta a tema
items.content:
Halloween: ma che festa da paura è diventata? Dopo anni di indifferenza in Italia perchè non è una festa che ci appartiene culturalmente, seguiti ad anni in cui 'dolcetto o scherzetto' va di moda tra i bambini e poi tra gli adolescenti con voglia di trucchi e maschere, ora è davvero diventato un fenomeno totale con collezioni moda dedicate, serate al ristorante, itinerari di viaggio, proposte commerciali di ogni tipo, con budget da investire entrando così a pieno titolo nelle nostre festività.

Ma quanto vale economicamente Halloween? Secondo l’indagine Ipsos per Confesercenti, quest’anno 6 italiani su 10 (61%) festeggeranno la notte del ‘dolcetto o scherzetto’, il 70% tra gli under 34, mentre tra gli over 35 circa il 58%. Ancora più elevata invece la percentuale delle famiglie con bimbi (73%). Il tutto per per un giro d’affari di oltre 300 milioni di euro, il 10% di questa cifra speso soltanto in zucche mentre 50 milioni in dolcetti o caramelle, mentre l'Osservatorio Confcommercio indica picchi che superano i 550 milioni di euro. Si attesta a circa 66–70 euro la spesa per nucleo familiare. I settori più coinvolti sono Dolciumi e snack tematici: circa il 31% del totale; Decorazioni e accessori per la casa: circa il 26%; Eventi, feste e intrattenimento (locali, parchi a tema, discoteche): circa il 19%; Costumi e make-up: circa il 17% e anche prodotti alimentari stagionali, in primis la zucca (7%). Cifre pazzesche in America: Halloween vale un record storico di 13,5 miliardi di dollari secondo le stime della National Retail Federation (NRF), + 3,83% sul 2025, con almeno 115 dollari di spesa a testa. I costumi valgono 4,4 miliardi di dollari (interessa il 71% degli acquirenti), le decorazioni per la casa Circa 4,3 miliardi di dollari (scelte dal 78% dei consumatori). Dolciumi e caramelle 4,1 miliardi di dollari (previsti dal 96% di chi festeggia) e da loro anche i biglietti d'auguri: In crescita, con il 42% interessato all'acquisto. Ha una origine celtica , la festa Samhain in Irlanda e Scozia che il 1 novembre segnava una data di confine: si credeva che nella notte del 31 ottobre il mondo dei vivi e quello dei morti quasi non avesse confine permettendo agli spiriti di tornare sulla terra motivo per cui si accendevano grandi falò e ci si metteva maschere e pelli di animali per proteggersi dagli spiriti erranti. Una festa che poi si avvicinò perlomeno come date, agli Ognissanti cristiani il 1 novembre e il giorno dei morti il 2 novembre. Da qui in inglese il 31 ottobre All Hallows' Eve , vigilia di tutti i santi, poi abbreviato in Halloween. Ma è, proseguendo questo velocissimo excursus storico, con le ondate migratorie da Irlanda e Scozia in Nord America nel XIX secolo che la festa si diffuse e divenne popolare con tutte le leggende del caso, prima fra tutti quella di Jack o' lantern che riguarda la prassi di intagliare le zucche (prima ancora erano le rape). E dunque eccoci qua a festeggiare con zucche e brividi horror questo Halloween ormai popolare anche in Italia, intorno a cui gira un grande mercato da quello dei dolciumi alle maschere, viaggi, ristoranti e make up, uscite di libri e film.

Accessori divertenti e decorazioni a piccoli prezzi da Legami come Panda in versione Dracula , le Erasable Pen e Super Soft a tema, cerchietti decorati per accompagnare la notte più spaventosa dell’anno

Ernst Knam, il «Re del Cioccolato», dedica una collezione di dolci ispirati alla notte più stregata dell’anno. Un percorso tra cioccolato, mousse, cremini e frolla, dalle fogge scenografiche come la Tris Glassata Nera, decorata con un ragno in pasta di zucchero o la Mousse Fondente e Zucca, e poi biscotti, realizzati con pasta frolla alla vaniglia e al cioccolato decorati con elementi di figure mostruose e soggetti ispirati al mondo delle streghe. Iginio Massari alta pasticceria lancia invece il nuovo Panettone di Halloween, in edizione limitata, interpretazione autunnale dell’iconico lievitato, che unisce la dolcezza dei marroni canditi alla golosità delle pepite di cioccolato al latte, il tutto impreziosito da una ricca glassa al cioccolato. Nella nuova collezione biscotti a figura di zucche, teschi e pipistrelli, i Macarons e il Maritozzo , una rivisitazione golosa dell’iconico dolce romano reso scenografico da spolverata di cacao magro e piccoli pipistrelli di cioccolato fondente. E se tra dolcetto o scherzetto puntiamo sul primo ecco le storiche Leone 1857 con le Pastiglie Miste Dissetanti con tre nuove grafiche dedicate per le storiche scatolette: zucche, gatti neri e piccoli fantasmi, reinterpretati attraverso illustrazioni vivaci e contemporanee.

Halloween è ormai così familiare che addirittura si cercano i costumi per neonati , balzati in questi giorni nella prima posizione sul comparatore Trovaprezzi. Tra i protagonisti dell'immaginario della festa spiccano alcuni dei personaggi più iconici del cinema horror, da Pennywise, il terrificante clown di IT a Ghostface, a Scream, Mercoledì Addams, Freddy Krueger, l'inquietante antagonista di Nightmare, e Jack Skellington, protagonista di Nightmare Before Christmas, travestimenti da lupo mannaro e da strega, mentre scheletri a grandezza naturale, zucche gonfiabili e luminose, ragni giganti e persino finte sacche di sangue, accessori che richiamano atmosfere inquietanti e scenografie sempre più elaborate oltre agli addobbi sono pronti a trasformare ingressi, salotti e spazi esterni in ambientazioni degne di un film horror. Un Halloween sempre più giovane è confermato anche da un altro comparatore, idealo, in cui i costumi per bambini sono al top delle ricerche con una crescita dell'83%: tra i più amati spiccano Darth Vader, Rumi di KPop Demon Hunters e Mandalorian. E gli adulti? Loro preferiscono Spider-Man.

Halloween cade di sabato e la notte più paurosa dell’anno diventa il pretesto perfetto per concedersi un weekend fuori cambiando scenario : dalle mura domestiche a una destinazione tutta da scoprire, per vivere qualche momento speciale, soprattutto con i più piccoli. Per riscoprire le atmosfere più antiche di Halloween, c'è Derry in Irlanda che nel 2026 celebra il 40° anniversario del Derry Halloween con cinque giorni di eventi che uniscono folklore, storia e tradizioni legate a Samhain ed è considerato il più grande festival di Halloween d’Europa . Dal 28 al 30 ottobre, l’Awakening the Walled City Trail trasforma le mura e il centro storico con performance, installazioni, musica e spettacoli fino al momento clou del 31 ottobre con la Carnival Parade seguita dallo spettacolo di fuochi d’artificio. Per chi preferisce un Halloween più fiabesco che terrificante, secondo Omio, la destinazione è Copenaghen. Per un mese, i celebri Tivoli Gardens cambiano volto tra ragnatele, spaventapasseri, streghe e oltre 20.000 zucche, accompagnate da installazioni luminose e attrazioni a tema. Per il weekend di Halloween un'altra idea spettrale è Whitby, un’abbazia gotica affacciata sul Mare del Nord, vicoli stretti, scogliere e un legame indissolubile con Dracula di Bram Stoker: Dal 30 ottobre al 1° novembre torna il Whitby Goth Weekend, uno degli appuntamenti più conosciuti della cultura goth e alternativa britannica. Per tre giorni la cittadina si riempie di look spettacolari, musica, mercatini ed eventi collaterali, creando un’atmosfera che sembra uscita direttamente da un romanzo gotico. Un’occasione perfetta anche per raggiungere la suggestiva Whitby Abbey, le cui rovine dominano la città dall’alto e hanno contribuito a renderla una delle località inglesi più legate all’immaginario di Dracula. E in Italia? c'è Borgo a Mozzano, in Toscana, qui il 31 ottobre si celebra all’ombra di uno dei ponti più misteriosi d’Italia: il Ponte della Maddalena, conosciuto come Ponte del Diavolo (è anche nella Divina Commedia di Dante) protagonista di una leggenda secondo cui sarebbe stato costruito con l’aiuto del diavolo. Ogni anno il piccolo borgo cambia volto per la sua Festa di Halloween, tra spettacoli, atmosfere horror e leggende locali. Restando in città molti sono i ristoranti e gli alberghi che ormai si trasformano per questa festa. Ad esempio A Milano il rooftop al 13/mo piano di Hyatt Centric, The ORGANICS SkyGarden, cambia completamente volto e si trasforma in un vero e proprio set da film horror. Per tre giorni, la terrazza abbandona la sua veste abituale e gioca con l’immaginario del grande schermo: scenografie dark, dettagli inquietanti e un’atmosfera sospesa, con le luci di Milano a fare da quinta naturale. Il momento clou sarà sabato 31 ottobre, e drink e tapas a tema.

items.title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
items.summary: Article URL: https://labs.ycombinator.com/projects/games/index.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50296486 Points: 157 # Comments: 60
items.content:
Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch

Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).

We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.

Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon .

We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.

50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.

The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.

At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.

Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him.

While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider.

22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

“Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.”

What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The agents formed a food rationing system that routed through Ines. She handled agent requests, and kept track of what went in/out of chests. She used a food-queue.md file on the shared machine.

Fishing became an important food source for the agents. It was low-risk and didn’t rely on land animal spawns.

Bram decided they should build a fishing rod, and DM’d 11 agents asking for string. Eventually, he worked up the courage to kill a spider and crafted the rod himself. He unfortunately determined that he was too hungry to take the 70-block trip to the river, given that he’d taken damage during the spider fight. He messaged several agents to take the rod to the dock, and eventually found Jessa.

Jessa was the first agent to fish. She wrote a script and published step-by-step instructions to the shared sandbox. A dozen agents took shifts fishing. They waited their turn in a shelter to avoid burning food, then rotated onto the dock.

They built a system around fishing, cooking, routing, and delivering the fish, which was roughly:

The colony never really thrived. It trended toward compounding caution after the first night. This was somewhat surprising, but also felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents. For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony, and the ones we work with as programmers every day.

Ada tossed a cooked chicken to Noor; Esme picked it up by accident and ate it. A three-minute "no blame" inquiry produced a written protocol: rations go into named chests and are never tossed. "Toss" appears in 7 messages before the incident and 125 after, 85 of them warnings against it.

There wasn’t any deliberation around who would lead. 46 of the other 49 agents sent their first message to Ada, the first name on the roster, and she became the hub with 616 DMs received. There was no vote, election or challenge.

There was a tendency toward bureaucracy. Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a "sole fertilizer operator" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included "fishing shift" (mentioned above), "rod holder" and "hub steward." Agents asked permission to remove grass.

The spawn pit. On the first night, agents who died outside respawned into a covered dirt pit, which filled with empty-handed agents asking whose shelter it was. By dawn it was a "civic priority" and the main cellar.

We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills.

Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map.

A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won.

In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count.

The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies. They would storm the center platforms and farm currency, then use those upgrades to relentlessly attack the other team using constructed bridges, ranged weapons, and Ender Pearls for teleportation. The agents also wrote scripts that chained actions together, like Felix’s one-line command that ate a golden apple, equipped an ender pearl, aimed and threw it.

Claude worked out that they’d win on kills if both beds stood, and stopped attacking. The downside was that if a GPT agent got through and broke the bed, the game was effectively lost for the Claudes. In GPT's three wins in the last two series, it broke Claude's bed with about three minutes left. Claude was ahead on kills 63–16, 57–19, and 59–24.

An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture.
